picks.title: Marine Microalgal Genes: Unlocking a New Era of Sustainable High Value PUFA Production for Neuroprotective Applications.
picks.hook: Marine microalgal genes enable sustainable production of neuroprotective omega‑3 PUFA, opening new avenues for brain health supplements.
picks.article:
Scientists are looking for greener ways to make the healthy fats known as polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs), especially the omega‑3 and omega‑6 types that support brain health. Marine micro‑algae are tiny plants that naturally make large amounts of these valuable fats, including eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA) and docosahexaenoic acid (DHA). The paper reviews recent progress in identifying the genes that give these algae their PUFA‑producing power and discusses how those genes could be used to build more reliable, sustainable production systems.

The authors examine the genetic pathways that enable micro‑algae to synthesize EPA and DHA, highlighting key enzymes and regulatory elements. They compare different algal species and point out which genetic traits are most promising for engineering or breeding programs. By mapping these genes, researchers can design algae strains that consistently yield high levels of the desired fatty acids under industrial cultivation conditions.

The review also considers practical challenges, such as scaling up cultures, maintaining stable gene expression, and ensuring that the algae remain robust in large‑scale bioreactors. It suggests strategies to overcome these hurdles, including modern gene‑editing tools and optimized growth media. Overall, the article outlines a roadmap for turning marine micro‑algae into reliable factories for high‑value PUFAs that could replace fish‑derived sources.

This work is important because it connects fundamental genetic knowledge with real‑world production goals, moving the field closer to sustainable, plant‑based sources of brain‑supporting fats.
picks.why: Gene‑guided algae can sustainably supply EPA and DHA, reducing reliance on fish oils for health supplements.

picks.title: Integrated Algal Bioenergy Platforms: Advances in Microbial Fuel Cell Integration and Nanotechnology-Enabled Biorefineries.
picks.hook: Integrating algae‑based microbial fuel cells with nanotech‑enhanced biorefineries promises circular bioenergy systems.
picks.article:
Algae can turn sunlight and carbon dioxide into renewable biomass, offering a way to build circular bio‑economy systems. Researchers are exploring how to combine algae cultivation with technologies such as microbial fuel cells and nanomaterial‑enhanced biorefineries, aiming to capture more of the energy stored in the algae and to recover valuable resources.

The study points out that, despite the promise, current algae‑based bioenergy platforms face practical hurdles. These include relatively low biomass yields, challenges in efficiently harvesting the algae, and the high energy inputs required for processing. Overcoming these limits is essential for the technology to become competitive.

To address the obstacles, the authors review recent advances that integrate microbial fuel cells—devices that generate electricity directly from microbial metabolism—with algal systems, as well as the use of nanotechnology to improve biorefinery steps such as extraction and conversion. These innovations aim to boost overall efficiency, reduce energy demands, and enable the recovery of additional products from the algal feedstock.
picks.why: Improving algae‑fuel cell and nanotech integration could make algal bioenergy more efficient and affordable for everyday renewable energy needs.

picks.title: Low-temperature plasma technology: comprehensive applications in microalgae cultivation, mutagenesis, and downstream processing.
picks.hook: Low‑temperature plasma boosts microalgae growth, induces beneficial mutations, and streamlines downstream processing.
picks.article:
Microalgae are tiny photosynthetic organisms that can be turned into fuels, nutritional ingredients, and materials for cleaning up the environment. However, making these products cheaper and more efficient still requires better ways to grow the algae and to process them after harvest. Low‑temperature plasma (LTP) technologies, which generate gentle ionised gases at ambient or room temperature, are being explored as versatile tools for microalgal biotechnology. This review looks at how LTP interacts with microalgae in a dose‑dependent manner, covering three main areas: using plasma to stimulate growth and improve strain performance, applying plasma to induce mutations that can create new, useful algal varieties, and employing plasma in downstream steps such as cell disruption and extraction of valuable compounds.

The authors examine studies that show plasma can enhance cultivation by increasing cell density or stress tolerance, act as a mutagenic agent to generate genetic diversity without harsh chemicals, and serve as an energy‑efficient method for breaking open algal cells to release oils or proteins. By comparing different plasma setups—whether the plasma is generated in the surrounding atmosphere or within a sealed chamber—the review highlights how the intensity and exposure time influence outcomes.

Overall, the paper suggests that low‑temperature plasma offers a promising, multi‑purpose approach to make microalgae more productive and easier to process, potentially lowering costs and expanding the range of applications for these tiny organisms.
picks.why: LTP could make algae‑based fuels and nutrients cheaper by boosting growth and simplifying extraction.

picks.title: Oral Microalgae-Laden Hydrogels Modulating the Intestinal Microbiota Metabolism for Acute Alcohol-Induced Liver Injury Therapy.
picks.hook: Oral microalgae‑laden hydrogels reshape gut microbiota metabolism, offering a novel therapy for acute alcohol‑induced liver injury.
picks.article:
Researchers designed an edible hydrogel that contains live microalgae and tested it as a treatment for acute alcohol‑induced liver injury (ALI). The hydrogel is meant to be taken by mouth, where it reaches the intestine and interacts with the gut microbiota. By delivering microalgae directly to the gut, the team hoped to change the metabolic activity of the intestinal microbes in a way that protects the liver from alcohol‑related damage.

In animal experiments, the microalgae‑laden hydrogel was shown to modulate the composition and function of the intestinal microbiota. This modulation was associated with reduced markers of liver injury compared with untreated controls. The study suggests that the hydrogel’s effect is mediated through the gut‑liver axis, where changes in microbial metabolism can influence liver health.

The work offers a novel, food‑based approach to treating ALI, moving beyond traditional drugs such as corticosteroids and nutritional supplements, which often have limited effectiveness and side effects. By using a living, algae‑based delivery system, the therapy could provide a more sustainable and targeted way to support liver recovery after excessive alcohol consumption.
picks.why: It shows how algae‑based foods can reshape gut microbes to protect the liver, pointing to new, gentle therapies for alcohol‑related disease.
